title: Pauri 4, sound: saachaa saahib
hook: saachaa saahib saach naae bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carefree Giver of pauri three. Your line was the giver never tires. Did you give one thing without keeping count? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

Back in camp three, we set an alarm five minutes early for the amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. That hour came from somewhere specific: this pauri, the fourth step of Japji. Today, before we get to the early hours, we hear how the pauri begins. And it begins with a sound you already know. Sach, from aad sach, the true, turns up twice in its very first line, in two different forms, like one word trying on two coats.
screen: `THE ALARM FIVE MINUTES EARLY.` → `IT CAME FROM THIS PAURI.` → `ONE WORD IN TWO COATS.`

segments.voice: The opening line: saachaa saahib, saach naae, bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Let's sound it. Saachaa: SAA-chaa, the true one. Saahib: SAA-hib, Master, Lord; the same sahib you hear in Japji Sahib and Guru Granth Sahib, a word of honor. Saach: the true again, this time about a name. Naae: NAA-ay, name. Bhaakhiaa: BHAA-khi-aa, spoken, expressed. Bhaau: rhymes with how, with a breath on the b; it means love. Apaar: a-PAAR, without limit, boundless. So you can hear the outline already: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love. Now listen to the sound. Saachaa, saahib, saach: the line opens with three s-sounds in a row, soft and steady, like someone walking up to a door. Then it opens out with bhaakhiaa bhaau, two bh sounds side by side, and ends on the wide, open vowel of apaar. From a narrow door into a very big room. Soon the pauri turns to questions: what can we offer, what words can we say? And then a line you've heard before: amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar, the early hours, the true name, reflecting on its greatness. Then another word we'll open tomorrow: nadar. For now, this pauri is a good one to say slowly, because its first line is almost a whole prayer in miniature: who the One is, what the Name is, and how it's spoken, with love and no limit.
screen: `SAACHAA SAAHIB — TRUE MASTER.` · `SAACH NAAE — TRUE NAME.` · `BHAAU APAAR — BOUNDLESS LOVE.` · `THE AMRIT VELA LINE.` · then, large: `PAURI FOUR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line with me, slowly, out loud if you can. Saachaa saahib, saach naae. Bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Again, a little slower, letting the s-sounds be soft and the last word open wide. Saachaa saahib, saach naae. Bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar. Once more, almost whispered. Then sit, and notice how your breath lengthened on apaar. Let it stay long. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ਸਾਚਾ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਸਾਚੁ ਨਾਇ ਭਾਖਿਆ ਭਾਉ ਅਪਾਰੁ ॥`

segments.voice: Pauri four. The fourth step of Japji, opening with saachaa saahib: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love.
Your line: saachaa saahib. Tonight, set that alarm five minutes early again, and say the line once as you do. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 169 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 4, MEANING: THE EARLY HOURS.`

howItsDone: The fourth pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its line on the amrit vela is the scriptural root of the Sikh practice of rising before dawn for simran.

match.prompt: match the sound to its sense.

myth: the amrit vela comes from Japji's fourth pauri
amrit vela sach naau vadiaaee veechaar.
saahib in this line is unrelated to Japji Sahib
it's the same word of honor: Master, Lord.
the first line uses the word for true only once
saachaa, saach: the true appears in more than one form.

fork.setup: the first line says the true Master's name is spoken a certain way. how?
fork.reveal: bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar: spoken with love that has no limit.

original.script: ਸਾਚਾ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਸਾਚੁ ਨਾਇ ਭਾਖਿਆ ਭਾਉ ਅਪਾਰੁ
original.say: SAA-chaa SAA-hib, SAACH NAA-ay, BHAA-khi-aa BHAU a-PAAR
original.note: Gurmukhi: the opening line of Japji's fourth pauri, Ang 2.

trapdoor: what you thought: true Lord, true name.
what it means: true Master, true name, spoken with boundless love: the line that leads to the amrit vela.
what a scholar hears: saahib comes into Punjabi from Arabic; bhaakhiaa, spoken, is kin to the Sanskrit bhasha, speech: both worlds in one line.

notes: Romanization and gloss of pauri 4's first line; 'bhaakhiaa bhaau apaar' is read by some as 'His language is boundless love'. Confirm preferred reading.
Saahib (Arabic sahib) and bhaakhiaa (cf. Sanskrit bhasha): confirm etymologies.
